title.en: Raja Suran Descends to the Sea-Kingdom in a Glass Chest
title.zh: 蘇蘭王乘玻璃櫃潛入海底王國

region.en: Southern Java Sea (symbolic pin — the open sea crossed between Kling and Tamsak)
region.zh: 爪哇南部海域（象徵性定位：克林與淡馬錫之間的公海）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (Raja Suran's descent), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Wishing to see the wonders of God's creation, Raja Suran seals himself in a locked glass chest lowered by a golden chain into the sea. He lands in the submarine realm of Zeya, marries the sea-king's daughter Putri Mahtab-al-Bahri, fathers three sons, and escapes upward on a flying, swimming sea-horse named Sambrani — the Malay Annals' charter myth of the dynasty's descent from the world under the water.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王欲一睹上帝造化之奇，乃自封於玻璃櫃中，繫以金鏈沉入海底。抵水下之境澤亞，娶海王之女瑪赫塔布，生三子；後騎能飛能泳之海馬桑布拉尼上歸人世——《馬來紀年》以此為王族出自水下世界之憲章神話。

sensitivity.note: Literary dynastic chronicle (Sejarah Melayu); Malaysian and Indonesian Malay communities hold the heritage; the text itself is public domain. Cross-cluster: descent to the otherworld parallels Inanna/Ishtar and Izanagi.

passages.text: Raja Suran, considering that he had now become acquainted with the contents of the land, wished to acquire information concerning the nature of the sea. For this purpose he ordered a chest of glass, with a lock in the inside, and fixed it to a chain of gold. Then, shutting himself up in this chest, he caused himself to be let down into the sea, to see the wonders of God Almighty's creation. At last the chest reached a land, denominated Zeya, when Raja Suran came forth from the chest and walked about to see the wonders of the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Zeya he found a people so numerous that God alone could know their numbers, and their king, Aktab-al-Arz, seated him upon his own throne and gave him his daughter, Putri Mahtab-al-Bahri, in marriage; by her he had three sons. At length Suran reflected what advantage it was to stay so long below the earth, and how he might carry his sons' line upward, for it would be a great disadvantage to cut off the line of Secander Zulkarneini.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: His father-in-law furnished him with a sea-horse named Sambrani, which could fly through the air as well as swim in the water. Suran mounted amid the lamentations of his spouse; the steed quickly cleared the nether atmosphere and rapidly traversed the upper ocean, where his followers perceived him, and by presenting a mare on the shore they lured Sambrani to land and recovered their king. Suran then commanded that the account of his descent be inscribed on a stone monument for posterity, to be found by one of his descendants who should reduce all the rajas under the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rusty Needles: China Cheats the Conqueror
title.zh: 生鏽的鐵針：中國以計退敵

region.zh: 淡馬錫（今新加坡一帶，《馬來紀年》地理）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (the ruse of the mantri of China), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When Raja Suran's immeasurable host threatens China, a sagacious mantri loads a prow with old, toothless sailors, seeds of bidara trees, and iron bars thick as an arm, all rusted over, and sends it to Tamsak. The 'traders' explain that they left China as children and have grown old on the voyage — so vast is the distance. Believing the world's measure, Suran turns back without a battle.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王大軍將犯中國，中國一賢臣獻計：以滿載老邁無齒水手、巴旦樹種與粗如臂之鐵條（皆已鏽蝕）之船駛至淡馬錫，訛稱自幼離華、行旅經年、樹已結實、鐵已鏽細——蘇蘭王信路途無涯，遂罷兵而返。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle fiction; an episode of ruse-warfare in the Malay Annals' Alexander-derived prehistory.

passages.text: It was reported in the land of China that Raja Suran was advancing with an innumerable army and had arrived at Tamsak. The raja of China was alarmed and said to his mantris and chieftains: 'If the Kling raja approach, the country will be inevitably ruined; what method do you advise to prevent his approach?' Then a sagacious mantri said: 'Lord of the world, your slave will fall on a device.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: He ordered a prow filled full of fine needles but covered with rust, planted with seeds of the casamak and bidara trees, and selected a party of old and toothless people to sail to Tamsak. When Suran's men asked how far it was to China, the Chinese replied: 'When we set sail we were all young, about twelve years of age, and we planted these seeds; now we have grown old and lost our teeth, and the seeds we planted have become trees which bore fruit before our arrival here.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: They took out some of the rusty needles and showed them, saying: 'When we left China these bars of iron were thick as your arm; now they have grown thus small by the corrosion of rust.' If the account were true, said Suran, the land of China must be at an immense distance — when should they ever arrive? All the champions assented, and Raja Suran turned back his host without a battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fall of Gangga Nagara: Suran and Ganggi Shah Juana
title.zh: 剛迦王國之陷落：蘇蘭對剛吉沙朱阿納

region.en: Gangga Nagara on the river Dinding, Perak (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 霹靂州丁丁河畔剛迦城（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (conquest of Gangga Nagara and Glang Kiu), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: On his march, Raja Suran breaks the steeps of Gangga Nagara with his chacra and duels its raja on elephant-back: Ganggi Shah Juana's arrow fells Suran's huge elephant, but Suran springs up and cuts off the defender's head. He marries the dead king's sister and rides on to destroy Glang Kiu and its raja Chulan in a mêlée of amokas — the Annals' grand old-war set piece.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王征途之中，以查克羅擊碎剛迦陡城之門，與守王於象背決鬥：剛吉沙朱阿納一箭射倒蘇蘭巨象，蘇蘭躍起拔劍斬其首。娶其妹剛迦公主，續而破翡翠之地格蘭基烏，陣斬朱蘭王——此乃《紀年》古戰史之壯闊段落。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle battle-legend; Perak (Malaysia) place-myth recorded within the shared Malay chronicle tradition.

passages.text: Raja Suran mounted his huge elephant and approached the gate of the fortress, notwithstanding the showers of spears and arrows with which he was assailed; he smote the gate with his chacra, and it immediately tumbled down, while the raja entered the fort with all his champions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Raja Ganggi Shah Juana seized his bow and smote the elephant of Raja Suran on the forehead, which instantly fell down. Raja Suran quickly sprang up and drew his sword, and smote off the head of Raja Ganggi Shah Juana; after the raja's death all his subjects submitted, and Suran married Putri Gangga, the beautiful sister of the slain king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Glang Kiu the place of the emerald, raja Chulan met him with a host like the sea rough with waves; elephants rushed against elephants, horses bit horses, and the dust ascended to the heavens till the day was darkened like an eclipse. Suran and Chulan charged each other on their elephants roaring like thunder; Chulan's spear pierced Suran's elephant from side to side, and Suran's arrow struck Chulan on the breast and pierced him to the back, and Chulan fell dead on his elephant. Suran took to wife his daughter, Putri Onang-kiu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Bichitram Shah Abandons His Kingdom for the Sea

region.en: The sea of Silbou (symbolic pin, western Malay world)
region.zh: 西爾布之海（象徵性定位，馬來世界西部）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (Bichitram Shah's fleet), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Angry that his father Raja Suran gave him only a small territory while his brothers received kingdoms, Bichitram Shah embarks with twenty war-vessels to conquer the maritime lands. After taking scores of countries he reaches the sea of Silbou, where a hurricane scatters his fleet: half returns to Chandukani, the fate of the other half is unknown — the Annals' template of the sea-faring prince from whom the Palembang line will later descend.
summary.zh: 父王蘇蘭僅予小邑，比奇特蘭沙憤而率二十艘戰船出海，征服海上諸邦；至西爾布海遇風暴，船隊四散——半數歸于昌杜卡尼，半數下落不明。《紀年》以此為海上王侯漂泊之母題，日後巴鄰旁王系即出其後。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; fine as a comparative 'hero on the sea' motif record.

passages.text: On his eldest son Bichitram Shah, Raja Suran only conferred a territory of small extent; and the young prince being displeased at this measure, resolved to abandon his country. He embarked with twenty vessels fitted out with all the apparatus of war, determining to conquer all the maritime districts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: After conquering several scores of countries, he at last reached the sea denominated Silbou, where, being caught in a dreadful hurricane, his fleet was dispersed, and the half of them returned to the country of Chandukani, but the fate of the other half is unknown. The adventures of this prince were very numerous, but they are only alluded to briefly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rice That Turned to Gold on the Mountain of Belidung

region.en: Mount Sagantang Maha Miru, near Palembang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴鄰旁附近薩甘當摩訶米魯山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (Wan Ampu and Wan Malin), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Two rice-cultivating women of Belidung, Wan Ampu and Wan Malin, see their fields gleam like fire in the night. At dawn the grain has become gold, the leaves silver, the stalks brass — and on the golden ground stand three young men: Bichitram Shah's heir as Sang Sapurba on a white steer, with Nila Pahlawan and Karana Pandita holding sword and lance. The Annals' founding apparition of the Palembang dynasty, and the origin of the Awang and Dara castes.
summary.zh: 勿里洞二女萬阿木普與萬馬林耕稻於薩甘當山上，夜見田如火光；晨起視之，穀化金、葉化銀、稈化銅——金土之上立三少年：白牛背上的王儲（後稱三保爺·三蘇爾巴），持劍執矛二侍從立於兩側。此即巴鄰旁王系之顯聖神話，亦阿旺、達拉二姓之由來。

sensitivity.note: Dynasty-foundation apparition; Palembang and Minangkabau communities hold the heritage; public-domain source.

passages.text: There were two young women of Belidung, Wan Ampu and Wan Malin, employed in cultivating rice on this mountain, where they had large and productive rice-grounds. One night they beheld their rice-fields gleaming and glittering like fire; 'It is some great snake or naga,' said Malin, and they lay quiet for fear. When it was daylight they went to see what it was, and found the grain of the rice converted into gold, the leaves into silver, and the stalks into brass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the ground which had assumed this golden colour they saw three young and handsome men: one in the dress of a raja mounted on a bull white as silver, the others holding a sword and a spear. Asked whether they were Jins or Peris, the centre one answered that they were of the race of men, descendants of Raja Secander Zulkarneini and offspring of Raja Suran, whose crown was the evidence of their descent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The girls invited them home and cut the paddy for their food; the prince's name was changed to Sang Sapurba. The bull vomited foam, from which emerged a man named Bat'h, with an immense turban, who began to recite the prince's praises in the Sanscrit language, giving him the title Sang Sapurba Trimarti Tribhuvena. From Bat'h descend the original reciters of the cheritras; Nila Pahlawan and Karana Pandita married the two women, and their male offspring were called Baginda Awang and the female offspring Baginda Dara — hence the origin of all the Awangs and Daras.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Thirty-Nine Leprous Brides of Sang Sapurba
title.zh: 三蘇爾巴王的三十九位痲瘋新娘

region.en: Mount Sagantang Maha Miru, Palembang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩甘當山，巴鄰旁（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the leprosy of the low-born brides), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When the heaven-descended prince Sang Sapurba wishes to marry, local rajas bring their daughters — but thirty-nine brides of unsuitable rank are stricken with leprosy 'as with a plague sent as a curse' the moment they join him. Only Wan Sundaria, daughter of the Palembang raja Damang Lebar Dawn, of sufficiently noble blood, escapes untouched — the Annals' mythic warning that kingship of divine descent must be matched with royal blood.
summary.zh: 天降王子三蘇爾巴欲娶親，諸邦獻女——然門第不配者，一與王合即患痲瘋，凡三十九人，如遭天譴。惟巴鄰旁王女萬蘇達莉亞出身高貴，獨免於災——《紀年》以此警示：神裔之王必配王族之血。

sensitivity.note: Royal-hypogamy taboo in the Annals; flagged as interpretive — the leprosy curse encodes caste/royal endogamy rules.

passages.text: It was soon noised over the whole country that a descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini had descended on the mountain Sagantang Maha Miru, and all the rajas of the neighbouring countries came with rich presents to pay their respects to him. As he wanted to marry, they all brought him their daughters; but as they were not of proper rank for such a noble prince, as soon as they associated with him they were stricken with a leprosy, as with a plague sent as a curse, to the number of thirty-nine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The raja of Palembang had a daughter of extreme beauty, Wan Sundaria. Sang Sapurba sent to ask her in marriage; her father excused himself, alledging that she would probably be struck with sickness, and would only resign her on certain conditions. After the marriage it was found that she had escaped the curse of leprosy which had afflicted his former wives, to the raja's great satisfaction, and Damang Lebar Dawn came in great haste, rejoiced to find her in excellent health.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Covenant of Damang Lebar Dawn: Why a Malay Raja May Not Shame His People
title.zh: 達萬·勒巴爾道恩之盟約：馬來王何以不可羞辱其民

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the marriage conditions), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Before giving his daughter to Sang Sapurba, Damang Lebar Dawn imposes conditions binding both lines forever: his descendants shall serve the raja's line, but shall never be bound, shamed, or reviled — great faults punished only by death under law; while the raja's line shall never suffer treason from his people's descendants, on pain of heaven 'turning their authority upside down.' The Annals presents this mythic oath as the constitutional origin of Malay kingship and its corresponding loyalty.
summary.zh: 達萬·勒巴爾道恩嫁女之前與三蘇爾巴立盟：其後裔世奉王室，然永不受縛、不受辱、不受詈——重罪唯依法處死；而王系永不受其民後裔之叛，違者天罰顛覆其權。《紀年》以此神話之誓為馬來君權與臣忠之憲政起源。

sensitivity.note: Charter-myth of Malay constitutional custom (adat); the Annals states this oath as the origin of the no-shaming rule.

passages.text: The conditions were that on Sangsapurba marrying his daughter, all the family of Damang Lebar Dawn should submit themselves to him; but that Sangsapurba should engage, both for himself and his posterity, that they should receive a liberal treatment — that when they committed faults they should never be exposed to shame nor opprobrious language, but if their faults were great, that they should be put to death according to the law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sangsapurba requested in his turn that the descendants of Damang Lebar Dawn should never move treasonable practices against his descendants, even though they should become tyrannical. 'Very well,' said Damang Lebar Dawn, 'but if your descendants break your agreements, probably mine will do the same.' These conditions were mutually agreed to, and the parties swore to perform them, imprecating the divine vengeance to turn their authority upside down who should infringe these agreements.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: From this condition it is that none of the Malay rajas ever expose their Malay subjects to disgrace or shame; they never bind them, nor hang them, nor give them opprobrious language; for whenever a raja exposes his subjects to disgrace, it is the certain token of the destruction of his country: hence also it is that none of the Malay race ever engage in rebellion, or turn their faces from their own rajas, even though their conduct be bad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bathing-House of Seven Stories: Installation of Sang Sapurba
title.zh: 七層浴殿：三蘇爾巴的即位大典

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the royal bath), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: To celebrate the marriage that escaped the leprosy curse, Damang Lebar Dawn builds the seven-storied bathing-house Pancha Presadha, and for forty days and nights the country feasts until 'the heaps of half-burnt rice lay like hillocks' and buffalo heads float in seas of rice-broth like islands. The royal couple then circles the bath seven times, bathes on its highest story, and ascends the golden throne — the Annals' fullest picture of royal installation ritual.
summary.zh: 為慶婚姻之成，達萬·勒巴爾道恩建七層浴殿『五重寶』；四十晝夜大宴，燒半之米堆積如丘，牛首浮於米湯如島。王與后繞殿七匝，登最高層共浴，後易禮服登金座鳴鼓即位——此為《紀年》所載最詳之王室即位儀注。

sensitivity.note: Royal installation ritual narrative; the bath rite (bersalin) persisted in Malay courts.

passages.text: After his return to Palembang, Damang Lebar Dawn ordered a splendid bathing-house to be constructed, and the architect was the aforesaid Bat'h. This bathing house was named Pancha Presadha, and it had seven stories, and terminated in five towers on the roof. A public festival was then made for the space of forty days and forty nights, attended by all the inferior rajas, mantris, eunuchs, bantaras, champions, and commons in general.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The heaps of half-burnt rice rejected lay like hillocks, and the skimming of the foam of the rice-broth stood in little seas, in which floated the heads of buffaloes and goats like so many islands. After the completion of the forty days and nights, the bathing water was introduced with all kinds of music and an immense concourse of people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The husband and wife, with a great multitude, seven times encircled the bathing-house, and afterwards bathed in the highest story, Bat'h officiating at the bath. After bathing they changed their garments — Sangsapurba arraying himself in the derapata deremani and the queen in the burudaimani — then mounted the golden throne of authority, and the state drums were beat; Bat'h inserted the Panchawa Panchara on the temples of the royal pair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Putri Tunjong Bui, the Princess Born of a Foam-Bell
title.zh: 泡沫之鐘公主：敦戎布伊

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (Putri Tunjong-bui), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: One day the river of Palembang brings down a foam-bell of uncommon size, and within it appears a young girl of extreme beauty. Sang Sapurba adopts her as his daughter and names her Putri Tunjong Bui, the Princess Foam-Bell — the river-born daughter who will be given in marriage to the young Chinese noble left at court, linking the Palembang line to China.
summary.zh: 一日巴鄰旁河漂下一泡沫巨鐘，鐘中現一絕美少女。三蘇爾巴收為養女，名曰『泡沫之鐘公主』敦戎布伊——此河生之女後嫁留朝之中華貴胄，將巴鄰旁世系與中國相連。

sensitivity.note: Foundling-from-river motif in the dynastic chronicle.

passages.text: It happened on a certain day that the river of Palembang brought down a foam-bell of uncommon size, in which appeared a young girl of extreme beauty. The raja being informed of the circumstance ordered her to be brought to him; this was done, and the raja adopted her as his daughter. She was named Putri Tunjong-bui, or the Princess Foam-bell, and the prince was extremely fond of her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The young Chinese of noble birth who had remained at Palembang became greatly attached to the raja, and the raja to him; he wished to settle him in marriage with the Putri Tunjong-bui. The present rajas of Palembang, according to the chronicle, are all descended of this family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Signet Sent to China: A Marriage Alliance Across the Sea
title.zh: 送印之中國使節：跨海聯姻

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (marriage of Putri Sri Devi), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The raja of China, hearing that a heaven-descended raja reigns in Palembang, sends ten prows bearing three bahars of gold to ask for his daughter. The warriors counsel compliance 'to promote the friendship between the Malay and the Chinese rajas,' and the elder princess Sri Devi is sent north with a letter stamped with the signet Kampen — declaring that only letters bearing its counterpart may ever be trusted from the Malay line.
summary.zh: 中國王聞天裔之王在巴鄰旁，遣十船載三巴哈爾之金求娶公主。群臣議從，以敦馬中之誼；乃以長公主斯里提毗許嫁，附蓋『甘般』印信之國書——明示：惟印文相符者方可信為馬來王系之書。

sensitivity.note: Diplomatic myth in the Annals; part of the Chinese alliance cycle.

passages.text: It was now noised all over the world that the descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini was now in the land of Palembang, even so far as the land of China. Then the raja of China sent to Palembang ten prows to ask his daughter in marriage, bringing as presents three bahars of gold and a great quantity of articles of China, with male and female slaves to convey the raja's letter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The warriors were of opinion that if the request were not complied with the safety of the country would be endangered; besides, said they, there is no greater prince than the raja of China. Then Sangsapurba granted the request to promote the friendship between the Malay and the Chinese rajas, and the elder princess, Sri Devi, was delivered to the Chinese ambassador, together with a letter stamped with the signet Kampen, desiring that when a paper signed with a similar stamp should arrive in China, they might depend on its being sent by the Malay rajas, but not to credit any other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The raja of China was highly gratified with the daughter of the raja from the mountain Sagantang, and treated her with the dignity due to her rank; she in due time produced a son, from whom are descended the royal race who reign in China at the present time, says the chronicle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Fresh Water Within the Rotan Rings on the River of Cuantan

region.en: Mouth of the river Cuantan, Sumatra

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the fresh water of Cuantan), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Sailing in search of a new country, Sang Sapurba's exhausted fleet finds the river of Cuantan all salt water, with no fresh supply. The raja bids his crew tie rotans into circles and cast them on the water; descending into a small boat, he sets his feet inside the rings, and 'by the power of God Almighty and the virtue of a descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini' the water within the circles turns fresh. The Annals explains that to this day fresh and salt water mingle at that place.
summary.zh: 三蘇爾巴船隊溯瓜南河，淡水告罄。王命以藤結環投於水面，自乘小舟以足入環之內；『憑上帝之大能與亞歷山德羅王裔之德』，環內之水化為甘泉，全船得以汲飲。《紀年》云：至今其處淡鹹交錯。

sensitivity.note: Etiological place-myth of the chronicle, tied to the Minangkabau founding.

passages.text: Raja Sangsapurba arrived at the point of Balang, where he observed a river's mouth of very great extent: the river of Cuantan, whose country was extremely populous. It was represented to him that all the fresh water was exhausted, and that there was no place to obtain more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Raja Sangsapurba directed them to bring rotans and tie them in circles and throw them into the water; then having himself descended into a small boat, he inserted his feet into the water within the circles of bamboo, and by the power of God Almighty and the virtue of a descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini, the water within these circles became fresh, and all the crews supplied themselves with it, and unto this day the fresh water is mixed with the salt at this place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Sacatimuna the Serpent of Menangcabow and the Sword of One Hundred and Ninety Notches
title.zh: 米南加保之蛇薩卡蒂穆納與一百九十缺口的寶劍

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the killing of Sacatimuna), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The chiefs of Menangcabow, having no raja, will crown Sang Sapurba on one condition: that he destroy Sacatimuna, the immense serpent that no blade has ever stunned or wounded, which destroys their cultivation. His champion Peramas Cumambang advances with the sword Chora Samanda Kian; the serpent unfolds coils like a hillock and the champion cuts it in three — but the sword carries away one hundred and ninety notches, and the Pagaroyung dynasty is founded on the victory.
summary.zh: 米南加保諸酋無王，允立三蘇爾巴，惟一條件：誅其地巨蛇薩卡蒂穆納——凡刃不能傷、糟害田禾之蛇。王遣勇士珀拉馬斯執劍『卓拉·薩曼達基安』往討；蛇身盤曲如丘，勇士一劍斷為三截——然劍上留一百九十缺口。巴加爾容王朝即以此勝開基。

sensitivity.note: Dragon-slayer charter of Minangkabau kingship as told in the Annals; note the notched-sword detail (the monster's hide tests the hero's weapon).

passages.text: All the chief men of Menangcabow consulted about appointing him their raja, since they had none. Then the ancient chiefs desired them first to enquire if he would engage to kill the snake Sacatimuna which destroys all our cultivation; it had resisted all their efforts either to cut or pierce without either being stunned or wounded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: A champion named Peramas Cumambang was sent with his famous sword Chora Samanda Kian to perform this service. As soon as he approached the place, the snake, smelling a man, unfolded his coils; the champion saw it lying with huge coils like a hillock, and as the snake put itself in motion he smote it with the sword and cut it into three parts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: In this combat, however, the sword Chora Samanda Kian received one hundred and ninety notches. Then all the people of Cuantan appointed Sangsapurba their raja, and he was established raja of Menangcabow, and of him are descended all the generations of the rajas of Pagaroyung unto this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Storm That Would Not Cease Till the Crown Went Overboard

region.zh: 民丹與淡馬錫之間的海峽

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. III (the crossing to Tamasak), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Crossing from Bentan toward the white sands of Tamasak, Sang Nila Utama's galley is caught in a storm; the crew jettisons the baggage, then everything, yet the sea still rises until the master warns that only the diadem can save them. The crown goes over the side and the storm instantly ceases — the omen that the prince must land unadorned and win his kingdom by new means, the prelude to the founding of Singhapura.
summary.zh: 三尼拉·烏他馬自民丹渡海往淡馬錫白灘，途中風暴驟起；拋盡行李衣物，浪仍不息——直至舟師言：『非棄王冠不能救。』王冠一擲，風浪立平——此乃異兆：王子必須卸卻榮飾、以新法贏得國土，《獅城建立》之序曲。

sensitivity.note: Sea-omen episode in the Singapore founding narrative.

passages.text: As they were passing over, they were caught in a severe storm, and the vessels began to leak, and the crews were unable, after repeated exertions, to throw out the water. They were compelled to throw overboard the greater part of the baggage; the water nevertheless continued to gain ground, and every thing was thrown overboard till nothing now remained but the diadem.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the master addressed the Prince Sang Nila Utama, stating that the vessel could not support the weight of the diadem, and that if it was not thrown overboard the vessel could not be relieved. The prince ordered the diadem to be thrown overboard, when the storm ceased and the vessel rose in the water, and the rowers pulled her ashore, and Sang Nila Utama landed on the sands of Tamasak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Beast on the Sands: How Singhapura Got Its Name
title.zh: 沙灘上的異獸：獅子城命名之由

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. III (the lion of Tamasak), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Hunting on the plain near the river of Tamasak after the storm, Sang Nila Utama sees a swift, beautiful beast — red-bodied, black-headed, white-breasted, larger than a he-goat — that vanishes inland at the sight of people. No one can name it until the aged Damang Lebar Dawn declares it the singha, the lion of the ancient histories: 'this is a fine place, that contains so fierce and powerful an animal.' The prince settles there and names the country Singhapura, the Lion City.
summary.zh: 風暴之後，三尼拉·烏他馬在淡馬錫河畔平原行獵，見一異獸：身紅、首黑、胸白，捷美勝山羊，見人即遁入內陸。無人能名之，至老臣達萬·勒巴爾道恩言：『此即古史所載之辛哈（獅）。此地能容如此猛獸，必為吉壤。』王子遂居其地，名之曰辛哈補羅——獅子城。

sensitivity.note: The best-known Malay foundation myth (Singapore's name); recorded within the Annals' Palembang-Singapura-Malacca cycle.

passages.text: There they saw an animal extremely swift and beautiful, its body of a red colour, its head black and its breast white, extremely agile, and of great strength, and its size a little larger than a he-goat. When it saw a great many people, it went towards the inland and disappeared. Sang Nila Utama enquired what animal was this, but none could tell him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Till he enquired of Damang Lebar Dawn, who informed him that in the histories of ancient time the singha or lion was described in the same manner as this animal appeared. 'This is a fine place which contains so fierce and powerful an animal.' Then Sang Nila Utama directed that he should not return; the queen sent people, elephants and horses, and thus Sang Nila Utama settled the country of Tamasak, named it Singhapura, and reigned over it, panegyrized by Bat'h with the name of Sri Tri-buana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
